Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 8.pdf ---
BECS (Book E-Commerce System)
So basically what we're trying to do is get books selling 
online instead of however you guys are doing it now, just a 
simple site where people can come in, look through what's 
available, throw a few books in a cart and check out. Nothing 
crazy, I just want it to actually work and not be a headache 
to keep up with. Right now I think it's all kind of manual or 
scattered and there's no real way for someone to just browse 
and buy without someone in the middle handling it, so that's 
the itch we're trying to scratch here. 
 
Anybody coming to the site should be able to just make an 
account, that's it, no big verification process or anything, 
and once they're in they can search for books and see title, 
author, price, add stuff to their cart and go through 
checkout. Keep the search simple, just matching on the title 
and it has to be exact, nothing fancy like partial matches or 
letting people search by author, that's more than we need 
right now. Some of these people might want to sign up to get 
notified about promotions and deals, so let's call those folks 
members, and they're the ones who can use promo codes when 
they check out. I picture this being pretty bare-bones in 
terms of who can buy what, like one copy of each book per 
order is plenty, we don't need people stacking ten copies of 
the same thing in their cart. 
 
On my side of things, I need a way to manage the inventory, 
basically a login that lets me add new books, edit prices, see 
how much stock I've got, that kind of stuff. I also want the 
system to ping me, like an email or something, whenever a book 
is running low so I don't get caught without stock, unless 
I've told it not to bother for that particular book because 
maybe I'm discontinuing it. And I want to be able to set up 
these percentage-off promotions every now and then and have it 
just email all the members automatically when I create one. 
 
One thing I want to be upfront about, we don't need to 
actually process real credit cards or handle real money 
movement right now, just collect the card number as part of 
the checkout flow and spit out a receipt and keep a log of 
what was purchased, who bought it, when. The real payment 
processing piece is something for way later, not part of this. 
Same with security stuff, I know that sounds bad, but honestly 
for what we need right now I'm not worried about encryption or 
people forgetting passwords or whatever, that's not a 
priority, let's not spend time building password recovery or 
anything like that for now. 
 
There's only going to be one person managing the store, me 
basically, so don't worry about building out roles for 
multiple managers or anything fancy like that, and a manager 
should never also be a regular customer account, those are two 
separate hats. It just needs to run somewhere people can get 
to it through a normal browser, nothing exotic on the 
technical side, just something stable that people in here can 
pull up and use without issues.

Sistema: BECS (Book E-Commerce System)

Resumo executivo: BECS is a browser-based book e-commerce system intended to replace manual and scattered sales activities. It enables customers to create accounts, browse and search the book catalog, manage a shopping cart, submit simulated-payment orders, and receive receipts. Members may receive promotional emails and apply promotion codes. A single store manager can maintain books, prices, stock, low-stock alert settings, promotions, and purchase records.

Escopo: Provide online book catalog, ordering, promotion, inventory, and sales-record management through a standard web browser.
  Em escopo: Customer account registration and authentication
  Em escopo: Book catalog browsing and exact-title search
  Em escopo: Shopping cart with one copy of each book per order
  Em escopo: Checkout with card-number collection and no real payment processing
  Em escopo: Receipt generation and purchase logging
  Em escopo: Optional promotional membership
  Em escopo: Percentage-based promotion codes for members
  Em escopo: Book, price, and inventory management
  Em escopo: Configurable low-stock email alerts
  Em escopo: Automatic promotional emails to members
  Em escopo: Single-manager administration
  Fora de escopo: Real payment authorization, settlement, or money movement — deferred to a future version
  Fora de escopo: Partial-title and author-based search — explicitly excluded from the initial version
  Fora de escopo: Password recovery — explicitly deprioritized
  Fora de escopo: Complex customer or purchasing roles — not required
  Fora de escopo: Multiple manager accounts and manager-role hierarchy — only one manager is required
  Fora de escopo: Purchase of multiple copies of the same book in one order — prohibited by business policy
  Premissa: PA-01: Customers have access to a standard web browser and an internet connection.
  Premissa: PA-02: [INFERRED] Customers and the manager provide valid email addresses for system notifications.
  Premissa: PA-03: [INFERRED] An external email-delivery capability is available.
  Premissa: PA-04: [INFERRED] The manager maintains accurate prices and stock quantities.
  Premissa: PA-05: [INFERRED] Delivery, taxation, and shipping calculations are not required because they are not described in the scenario.
  Restrição: REST-01 (Business): Only one manager account may exist.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Business): A manager identity may not also hold a customer account.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Functional): Book search is limited to exact title matching.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Business): An order may contain no more than one copy of each book.
  Restrição: REST-05 (Integration): The initial version must not process or transfer real payments.
  Restrição: REST-06 (Project scope): Encryption is not required for v0.1 because it was explicitly deprioritized by the sponsor.
  Restrição: REST-07 (Technical): The system must be accessible through a standard web browser.
  Restrição: REST-08 (Functional): Password-recovery functionality is excluded from v0.1.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Site Visitor (Usuário primário): Browse available books and create a customer account without a complex verification process.
  STK-02 - Customer (Usuário primário): Search books, view book information, manage a cart, submit an order, and receive a receipt.
  STK-03 - Member (Usuário primário): Receive promotion notifications and apply valid promotion codes during checkout.
  STK-04 - Store Manager (Usuário primário): Maintain the catalog, prices, stock, low-stock alerts, promotions, and purchase records.
  STK-05 - Email Delivery Service (Stakeholder externo): [INFERRED] Receive properly addressed email requests for low-stock and promotional notifications.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Direct customer registration: A visitor may become a customer without completing an extended identity-verification process.
  RN-002 - Exact-title search: Book searches must match the complete title exactly; partial-title and author searches are not supported.
  RN-003 - Single copy per order: An order may contain no more than one copy of each distinct book.
  RN-004 - Optional membership: A customer becomes a member only by opting in to promotional notifications.
  RN-005 - Member-only promotion codes: Only members may receive and use promotion codes during checkout.
  RN-006 - Percentage-based promotions: Promotions reduce the eligible order amount by a defined percentage.
  RN-007 - Low-stock notification: The manager must be notified when a book reaches its defined low-stock threshold.
  RN-008 - Promotion distribution: Creating a promotion causes its details to be distributed to all current members.
  RN-009 - Simulated payment: Checkout collects a card number but does not authorize, capture, settle, or transfer real funds.
  RN-010 - Purchase traceability: Each completed order must preserve what was purchased, who purchased it, and when it was purchased.
  RN-011 - Single manager: The store is administered by exactly one manager.
  RN-012 - Account-role separation: The manager and customer roles must be represented by separate identities.
  RN-013 - Stock availability: [INFERRED] A book may be included in a completed order only when at least one copy is available.

Requisitos funcionais:
  RF-001 - Register customer account: The system shall register a customer account without an extended identity-verification process. [Must have]
  RF-002 - Authenticate customer: The system shall authenticate a registered customer using account credentials. [Must have]
  RF-003 - Authenticate manager: The system shall authenticate the single manager using manager credentials. [Must have]
  RF-004 - Enforce role separation: The system shall prevent the manager identity from being registered as a customer account. [Must have]
  RF-005 - Browse catalog: The system shall present the available book catalog to site visitors. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Display book information: The system shall display the title, author, and price of each cataloged book. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Search by exact title: The system shall return books whose complete title exactly matches the submitted search value. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Add book to cart: The system shall add one copy of an available book to the authenticated customer's cart. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Prevent duplicate book: The system shall reject an attempt to add a book already present in the same cart. [Must have]
  RF-010 - View cart: The system shall display the books and prices currently contained in the customer's cart. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Remove book from cart: [INFERRED] The system shall remove a selected book from the customer's cart. [Should have]
  RF-012 - Opt into membership: The system shall allow a customer to opt into promotional membership. [Should have]
  RF-013 - Apply promotion code: The system shall apply a valid percentage-based promotion code submitted by a member during checkout. [Should have]
  RF-014 - Reject non-member promotion use: The system shall reject promotion-code use by a customer who is not a member. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Calculate percentage discount: The system shall calculate the order discount using the percentage associated with the applied promotion. [Should have]
  RF-016 - Validate stock at checkout: The system shall reject checkout when any carted book has no available stock. [Must have]
  RF-017 - Collect card number: The system shall collect a card number as part of the checkout flow. [Must have]
  RF-018 - Create order: The system shall create an order without performing real payment processing. [Must have]
  RF-019 - Generate receipt: The system shall generate a receipt after successful order creation. [Must have]
  RF-020 - Log purchase: The system shall record the purchased books, customer identity, and purchase timestamp for each completed order. [Must have]
  RF-021 - Decrement stock: The system shall decrement the stock of each purchased book by one after order creation. [Must have]
  RF-022 - Add book: The system shall allow the authenticated manager to add a book to the catalog. [Must have]
  RF-023 - Edit book price: The system shall allow the authenticated manager to edit a book's price. [Must have]
  RF-024 - View stock: The system shall display the current stock quantity of each book to the authenticated manager. [Must have]
  RF-025 - Update stock: [INFERRED] The system shall allow the authenticated manager to update a book's stock quantity. [Must have]
  RF-026 - Configure low-stock threshold: [INFERRED] The system shall allow the manager to define a low-stock threshold for each book. [Should have]
  RF-027 - Disable book alert: The system shall allow the manager to disable low-stock notifications for a selected book. [Should have]
  RF-028 - Send low-stock alert: The system shall email the manager when an alert-enabled book reaches its low-stock threshold. [Should have]
  RF-029 - Create promotion: The system shall allow the authenticated manager to create a promotion containing a code and percentage discount. [Should have]
  RF-030 - Email promotion to members: The system shall email a newly created promotion to all current members. [Should have]
  RF-031 - View purchase log: [INFERRED] The system shall allow the authenticated manager to view completed purchase records. [Should have]

Requisitos não funcionais:
  RNF-001 (Performance Efficiency) - The system shall return catalog and exact-title search responses within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile under [TBD] 100 concurrent users. | Métrica: At least 95% of measured responses complete within 2 seconds under 100 concurrent users [TBD].
  RNF-002 (Performance Efficiency) - The system shall create an order and display its receipt within 3 seconds after checkout submission under [TBD] 100 concurrent users. | Métrica: At least 95% of valid checkout submissions complete within 3 seconds [TBD].
  RNF-003 (Reliability) - The system shall maintain monthly availability of at least [TBD] 99.5%, excluding scheduled maintenance. | Métrica: Monthly availability is at least 99.5% [TBD].
  RNF-004 (Compatibility) - The system shall support 100% of core customer and manager flows on the latest two stable versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari [TBD]. | Métrica: All defined core-flow test cases pass on 8 browser-version combinations [TBD].
  RNF-005 (Interaction Capability) - The system shall enable at least [TBD] 90% of first-time test participants to locate a book, add it to the cart, and submit checkout within 10 minutes without assistance. | Métrica: At least 90% task completion within 10 minutes [TBD].
  RNF-006 (Security) - The system shall require authenticated manager access for 100% of catalog, stock, promotion, and purchase-log administration operations. | Métrica: All unauthorized requests to manager operations are denied in the access-control test suite.
  RNF-007 (Functional Suitability) - The system shall calculate cart totals and percentage discounts with a maximum variance of [TBD] 0.01 currency unit from the reference calculation. | Métrica: Maximum calculation variance is 0.01 currency unit [TBD].
  RNF-008 (Reliability) - The system shall ensure that 100% of successfully created orders have a corresponding receipt, purchase record, and stock decrement. | Métrica: Zero inconsistent records across 1,000 simulated checkout transactions [TBD].
  RNF-009 (Performance Efficiency) - The system shall submit low-stock and promotional emails to the email-delivery service within [TBD] 60 seconds of the triggering event. | Métrica: At least 99% of email requests are submitted within 60 seconds [TBD].
  RNF-010 (Reliability) - The system shall restore catalog, account, stock, promotion, and purchase data from backup with a recovery point objective of [TBD] 24 hours and recovery time objective of [TBD] 4 hours. | Métrica: RPO does not exceed 24 hours and RTO does not exceed 4 hours [TBD].
  RNF-011 (Maintainability) - The system shall permit 100% of routine book-price and stock changes through the manager interface without source-code modification. | Métrica: All routine price and stock maintenance test cases complete without code or database-script changes.

Casos de uso:
  UC-001 - Register customer account | Ator: Site Visitor
    1. The visitor opens the registration function.
    2. The visitor submits the required account data.
    3. The system verifies that the identity is not assigned to the manager.
    4. The system creates the customer account.
    5. The system confirms registration.
  UC-002 - Find a book | Ator: Customer
    1. The customer opens the catalog.
    2. The system displays available books.
    3. The customer submits a complete book title.
    4. The system performs an exact-title match.
    5. The system displays the matching title, author, and price.
  UC-003 - Manage shopping cart | Ator: Customer
    1. The customer selects an available book.
    2. The customer requests that the book be added.
    3. The system verifies that the book is not already in the cart.
    4. The system adds one copy to the cart.
    5. The system displays the updated cart.
  UC-004 - Join promotional membership | Ator: Customer
    1. The customer opens membership preferences.
    2. The customer opts into promotional notifications.
    3. The system records the membership status.
    4. The system confirms enrollment.
  UC-005 - Complete checkout | Ator: Customer
    1. The customer opens checkout.
    2. The system validates stock for every carted book.
    3. The customer submits a card number.
    4. The system creates the order without contacting a payment processor.
    5. The system decrements stock by one for each purchased book.
    6. The system records the customer, books, and timestamp.
    7. The system generates and displays a receipt.
  UC-006 - Maintain book inventory | Ator: Store Manager
    1. The manager opens inventory management.
    2. The manager selects the add-book function.
    3. The manager submits the book data.
    4. The system creates the catalog entry.
    5. The system confirms the change.
  UC-007 - Configure low-stock alerts | Ator: Store Manager
    1. The manager selects a book.
    2. The manager defines its low-stock threshold.
    3. The manager enables low-stock notifications.
    4. The system stores the configuration.
    5. The system emails the manager when stock reaches the threshold.
  UC-008 - Create and distribute promotion | Ator: Store Manager
    1. The manager opens promotion management.
    2. The manager enters a promotion code and percentage.
    3. The system validates the promotion data.
    4. The system creates the promotion.
    5. The system submits a promotional email for every current member.
    6. The system confirms promotion creation.
  UC-009 - Review purchase log | Ator: Store Manager
    1. The manager opens the purchase log.
    2. The system retrieves completed purchase records.
    3. The system displays the purchased books, customer, and purchase timestamp.

Critérios de aceite:
  CA-001 - Dado a visitor identity that is not already registered and is not the manager, quando the visitor submits valid registration data, então the system creates exactly one customer account and displays a registration confirmation
  CA-002 - Dado the manager identity, quando registration as a customer is attempted, então the system rejects the request and creates no customer account
  CA-003 - Dado a catalog containing a book titled 'Example Book', quando the customer searches for the complete title 'Example Book', então the system displays that book with its title, author, and price
  CA-004 - Dado a catalog containing a book titled 'Example Book', quando the customer searches for 'Example', então the system returns no matching book
  CA-005 - Dado an authenticated customer, an available book, and a cart not containing that book, quando the customer adds the book, então the cart contains exactly one copy of the selected book
  CA-006 - Dado a cart already containing a book, quando the customer attempts to add the same book again, então the system rejects the request and the cart still contains exactly one copy
  CA-007 - Dado a cart containing a selected book, quando the customer removes that book, então the selected book no longer appears in the cart
  CA-008 - Dado an authenticated non-member customer, quando the customer opts into promotional membership, então the customer's membership status becomes active
  CA-009 - Dado an authenticated member with a valid 10% promotion code and an eligible cart subtotal of 100.00, quando the member applies the code, então the system applies a discount of 10.00 with a maximum variance of 0.01
  CA-010 - Dado an authenticated customer who is not a member, quando the customer submits a promotion code, então the system rejects the code and applies a discount of 0.00
  CA-011 - Dado an authenticated customer with an in-stock cart and a submitted card number, quando the customer confirms checkout, então the system creates one order without sending an authorization or settlement request to a payment processor
  CA-012 - Dado a cart containing at least one book with zero stock, quando the customer submits checkout, então the system creates no order and makes no stock decrement
  CA-013 - Dado a successfully created order, quando order creation completes, então the system displays a receipt within 3 seconds [TBD]
  CA-014 - Dado a successfully completed order, quando the purchase log is inspected, então exactly one record identifies the purchased books, customer, and purchase timestamp
  CA-015 - Dado a book with stock quantity 5 included in a successful order, quando the order is created, então the book's stock quantity becomes 4
  CA-016 - Dado an authenticated manager and valid book data, quando the manager submits the new book, então the system creates one catalog entry containing the submitted title, author, price, and stock
  CA-017 - Dado an authenticated manager and an existing book priced at 20.00, quando the manager changes its price to 25.00, então the catalog displays the book price as 25.00
  CA-018 - Dado an authenticated manager and an existing book with stock quantity 2, quando the manager updates the quantity to 10, então the inventory view displays a stock quantity of 10
  CA-019 - Dado an alert-enabled book with threshold 2 and current stock 3, quando a successful order reduces its stock to 2, então the system submits one low-stock email to the manager within 60 seconds [TBD]
  CA-020 - Dado a book whose low-stock alert is disabled, quando its stock reaches or falls below its configured threshold, então the system submits zero low-stock emails for that event
  CA-021 - Dado an authenticated manager and valid promotion data containing code SAVE10 and percentage 10, quando the manager creates the promotion, então the system stores one promotion with code SAVE10 and percentage 10
  CA-022 - Dado three current members and two non-member customers, quando the manager creates a promotion, então the system submits exactly three promotional emails and addresses none to non-members
  CA-023 - Dado an authenticated manager and at least one completed purchase, quando the manager opens the purchase log, então the system displays the purchase's books, customer identity, and timestamp

Glossário:
  BECS: Book E-Commerce System, the software specified by this document.
  Customer: A registered user permitted to browse books, maintain a cart, and submit orders.
  Member: A customer who has opted into promotional notifications and may use promotion codes.
  Store Manager: The single administrative user responsible for catalog, inventory, promotions, and purchase records.
  Exact-title search: A search that returns a book only when the submitted value matches its complete title.
  Promotion Code: A code associated with a percentage discount and usable only by members.
  Low-stock threshold: The configured stock quantity at which an enabled low-stock notification is triggered.
  Simulated payment: Checkout behavior that collects a card number without authorizing, capturing, settling, or transferring funds.
  Purchase Log: The persistent record of purchased books, the purchasing customer, and the purchase timestamp.
  Receipt: The order confirmation produced after successful checkout.

O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.

Para alguns sistemas (p. ex., aplicativos móveis), os requisitos podem ser coletados da

implícitos (p. ex., dados de uso, registros de defeitos) [MNJR2015], [GrDA2015].
3.1.4 Técnicas baseadas em artefatos (L3)
Artefatos são produtos do trabalho humano (também chamados de produtos de trabalho), 
como sistemas de TI, documentos, imagens, arquivos de áudio e vídeo etc. Alguns tipos 
desses produtos de trabalho são relevantes como fontes de requisitos. Normalmente, é uma 
tarefa demorada examinar detalhadamente os produtos de trabalho.
3.1.4.1 Arqueologia do sistema (L3)
A arqueologia de sistemas é uma técnica para obter informações sobre um novo sistema a 
partir da documentação, da interface do usuário ou do código de um sistema legado ou 
concorrente. Recomenda-se começar a analisar documentos como especificações, 
documentação de teste ou manuais do usuário primeiro, pois eles contêm informações 
semelhantes aos requisitos. Com a ajuda da arqueologia do sistema, é possível garantir que 
nenhum requisito implementado no sistema atual seja perdido.
3.1.4.2 Leitura baseada em perspectiva (L3)
O Engenheiro de Requisitos usa uma perspectiva específica, por exemplo, perspectiva de 
uso ou perspectiva de dados, para recuperar requisitos relevantes de um documento 
[Pohl2010].
3.1.4.3 Reutilização de requisitos (L3)
Se houver projetos semelhantes ou versões anteriores do sistema a ser desenvolvido na 
empresa, os requisitos desses projetos poderão ser reutilizados. Os requisitos considerados 
para reutilização devem ser confirmados por meio de revisão ou técnicas adicionais de 
elicitação.

1.2 Engenharia de Requisitos: Porquê (L2)
A ER adequada agrega valor no processo de desenvolvimento e evolução de um sistema:
▪ Reduzindo o risco de desenvolver o sistema errado
▪ Melhorando a compreensão do problema
▪ Sendo base na estimativa de esforço e custo de desenvolvimento
▪ Sendo pré-requisito no teste de sistema
Sintomas típicos de uma ER inadequada são requisitos não especificados, sem clareza ou 
incorretos. Isto é particularmente devido a:
▪ Pressa para construção do sistema
▪ Problemas de comunicação entre stakeholders
▪ O pressuposto de que os requisitos são evidentes por si mesmos
▪ Capacitação e competências inadequadas na ER
1.3 Engenharia de Requisitos: Onde (L2)
A ER pode ser aplicada aos requisitos de qualquer sistema. No entanto, a aplicação 
dominante da ER hoje é basicamente em sistemas nas quais o software desempenha um 
papel importante. Tais sistemas normalmente consistem em componentes de software, 
elementos físicos e organizacionais.
Os requisitos podem ocorrer como:
▪ Requisitos do sistema - o que um sistema deve fazer
▪ Requisitos de stakeholders - o que os stakeholders querem de sua perspectiva
▪ Requisitos de usuário - o que os usuários querem de sua perspectiva
▪ Requisitos de domínio - propriedades de domínio necessárias
▪ Requisitos de negócio - metas de negócio, objetivos, e necessidades de uma 
organização
1.4 Engenharia de Requisitos: Como (L1)
As principais tarefas na ER são a elicitação (4.2), documentação (3), validação (4.4) e 
gerenciamento (6) de requisitos. O uso de ferramentas (7) pode ajudar a realizar estas 
tarefas. A análise de requisitos e a resolução de conflitos de requisitos (4.3) são 
considerados parte da elicitação. Para executar corretamente as atividades da ER, um 
processo da ER deve ser adaptado a partir de um leque de possibilidades (5).

Consider building a catalog of user classes that recur across multiple applications. Defining user 
classes at the enterprise level lets you reuse those user class descriptions in future projects. The next 
system you build might serve the needs of some new user classes, but it probably will also be used 
by user classes from your earlier systems. If you do include the user-class descriptions in the project’s 
SRS, you can incorporate entries from the reusable user-class catalog by reference and just write 
descriptions of any new groups that are specific to that application.
User personas
To help bring your user classes to life, consider creating a persona for each one, a description of a 
representative member of the user class (Cooper 2004; Leffingwell 2011). A persona is a description 
of a hypothetical, generic person who serves as a stand-in for a group of users having similar 
characteristics and needs. You can use personas to help you understand the requirements and to 
design the user experience to best meet the needs of specific user communities.
A persona can serve as a placeholder when the BA doesn’t have an actual user representative 
at hand. Rather than having progress come to a halt, the BA can envision a persona performing 
a particular task or try to assess what the persona’s preferences would be, thereby drafting a 
requirements starting point to be confirmed when an actual user is available. Persona details for a 
commercial customer include social and demographic characteristics and behaviors, preferences, 
annoyances, and similar information. Make sure the personas you create truly are representative of 
their user class, based on market, demographic, and ethnographic research.
Here’s an example of a persona for one user class on the Chemical Tracking System:
Fred, 41, has been a chemist at Contoso Pharmaceuticals since he received his Ph.D. 
14 years ago. He doesn’t have much patience with computers. Fred usually works 
on two projects at a time in related chemical areas. His lab contains approximately 
300 bottles of chemicals and gas cylinders. On an average day, he’ll need four new 
chemicals from the stockroom. Two of these will be commercial chemicals in stock, 
one will need to be ordered, and one will come from the supply of proprietary Contoso 
chemical samples. On occasion, Fred will need a hazardous chemical that requires 
special training for safe handling. When he buys a chemical for the first time, Fred 
wants the material safety data sheet emailed to him automatically. Each year, Fred will 
synthesize about 20 new proprietary chemicals to go into the stockroom. Fred wants 
a report of his chemical usage for the previous month to be generated automatically 
and sent to him by email so that he can monitor his chemical exposure.
As the business analyst explores the chemists’ requirements, he can think about Fred as the archetype 
of this user class and ask himself, “What would Fred need to do?” Working with a persona makes the 
requirements thought process more tangible than if you simply contemplate what a whole faceless 
group of people might want. Some people choose a random human face of the appropriate gender 
to make a persona seem even more real.108 PART II Requirements development
Dean Leffingwell (2011) suggests that you design the system to make it easy for the individual 
described in your persona to use the application. That is, you focus on meeting that one (imaginary) 
person’s needs. Provided you’ve created a persona that accurately represents the user class, this 
should help you do a good job of satisfying the needs and expectations of the whole class.

Each user class will have its own set of requirements for the tasks that members of the class must 
perform. There could be some overlap between the needs of different user classes. Tellers, business 
bankers, and loan officers all might have to check a bank customer’s account balance, for instance. 
Different user classes also could have different quality expectations, such as usability, that will drive 
user interface design choices. New or occasional users are concerned with how easy the system is to 
learn. Such users like menus, graphical user interfaces, uncluttered screen displays, wizards, and help 
screens. As users gain experience with the system, they become more interested in efficiency. They 
now value keyboard shortcuts, customization options, toolbars, and scripting facilities.
Trap Don’t overlook indirect user classes. They won’t use your application themselves, 
instead accessing its data or services through other applications or through reports. Your

User classes need not be human beings. They could be software agents performing a service on 
behalf of a human user, such as bots. Software agents can scan networks for information about goods 
and services, assemble custom news feeds, process your incoming email, monitor physical systems 
and networks for problems or intrusions, or perform data mining. Internet agents that probe websites 
for vulnerabilities or to generate spam are a type of disfavored non-human user class. If you identify 
these sorts of disfavored user classes, you might specify certain requirements not to meet their needs 
but rather to thwart them. For instance, website tools such as CAPTCHA that validate whether a user is 
a human being attempt to block such disruptive access by “users” you want to keep out.
Remember, users are a subset of customers, which are a subset of stakeholders. You’ll need to 
consider a much broader range of potential sources of requirements than just direct and indirect user 
classes. For instance, even though the development team members aren’t end users of the system 
they’re building, you need their input on internal quality attributes such as efficiency, modifiability, 
portability, and reusability, as described in Chapter 14, “Beyond functionality.” One company 
found that every installation of their product was an expensive nightmare until they introduced an 
“installer” user class so they could focus on requirements such as the development of a customization 
architecture for their product. Look well beyond the obvious end users when you’re trying to identify 
stakeholders whose requirements input is necessary.

If you’re replacing an old system, you have an opportunity to document 
the requirements for the new one and to keep the requirements up to date with what you learn 
throughout the project. Try to leave the requirements in better shape than you found them.
Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Rarely do you need to document the entire existing system. Focus detailed requirements efforts 
on the changes needed to meet the business objectives. If you’re replacing a system, start by 
documenting the areas prioritized as most important to achieve the business objectives or those that 
pose the highest implementation risk. Any new requirements identified during the gap analysis will 
need to be specified at the same level of precision and using the same techniques as you would for a 
new system.
Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.
I worked with one team that was just beginning to develop the requirements for version 2 of 
a major product with embedded software. They hadn’t done a good job on the requirements for 
version 1, which was currently being implemented. The lead BA wondered, “Is it worth going back 
to improve the SRS for version 1?” The company anticipated that this product line would be a major 
revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line.

The voiceless user class
A business analyst at Humongous Insurance was delighted that an influential user, Rebecca, 
agreed to serve as product champion for the new claims processing system. Rebecca had many 
ideas about the system features and user interface design. Thrilled to have the guidance of an 
expert, the development team happily complied with her requests. After delivery, though, they 
were shocked to receive many complaints about how hard the system was to use.
Rebecca was a power user. She specified usability requirements that were great for experts, 
but the 90 percent of users who weren’t experts found the system unintuitive and difficult to 
learn. The BA didn’t recognize that the claims processing system had at least two user classes. 
The large group of non–power users was disenfranchised in the requirements and user interface 
design processes. Humongous paid the price in an expensive redesign. The BA should have 
engaged at least one more product champion to represent the large class of nonexpert users.
Selling the product champion idea
Expect to encounter resistance when you propose the idea of having product champions on your 
projects. “The users are too busy.” “Management wants to make the decisions.” “They’ll slow us down.” 
“We can’t afford it.” “They’ll run amok and scope will explode.” “I don’t know what I’m supposed to 
do as a product champion.” Some users won’t want to cooperate on a project that will make them 
change how they work or might even threaten their jobs. Managers are sometimes reluctant to 
delegate authority for requirements to ordinary users.
Separating business requirements from user requirements alleviates some of these discomforts. As 
an actual user, the product champion makes decisions at the user requirements level within the scope 
boundaries imposed by the business requirements. The management sponsor retains the authority 
to make decisions that affect the product vision, project scope, business-related priorities, schedule, 
or budget. Documenting and negotiating each product champion’s role and responsibilities give 
candidate champions a comfort level about what they’re being asked to do. Remind management 
that a product champion is a key contributor who can help the project achieve its business objectives.

If you encounter resistance, point out that insufficient user involvement is a leading cause of 
software project failure. Remind the protesters of problems they’ve experienced on previous projects 
that trace back to inadequate user input. Every organization has horror stories of new systems that 
didn’t satisfy user needs or failed to meet unstated usability or performance expectations. You 
can’t afford to rebuild or discard systems that don’t measure up because no one understood the 
requirements. Product champions provide one way to get that all-important customer input in a 
timely way, not at the end of the project when customers are disappointed and developers are tired.
Product champion traps to avoid
The product champion model has succeeded in many environments. It works only when the product 
champions understand and sign up for their responsibilities, have the authority to make decisions 
at the user requirements level, and have time available to do the job. Watch out for the following 
potential problems:
■ Managers override the decisions that a qualified and duly authorized product champion 
makes. Perhaps a manager has a wild new idea at the last minute, or thinks he knows what the 
users need. This behavior often results in dissatisfied users and frustrated product champions 
who feel that management doesn’t trust them.
■ A product champion who forgets that he is representing other customers and presents only 
his own requirements won’t do a good job. He might be happy with the outcome, but others 
likely won’t be.
■ A product champion who lacks a clear vision of the new system might defer decisions to the 
BA. If all of the BA’s ideas are fine with the champion, the champion isn’t providing much help.
■ A senior user might nominate a less experienced user as champion because she doesn’t have 
time to do the job herself. This can lead to backseat driving from the senior user who still 
wishes to strongly influence the project’s direction.
Beware of users who purport to speak for a user class to which they do not belong. Rarely, an 
individual might actively try to block the BA from working with the ideal contacts for some reason. 
On the Chemical Tracking System, the product champion for the chemical stockroom staff—herself 
a former chemist—initially insisted on providing what she thought were the needs of the chemist 
user class. Unfortunately, her input about current chemist needs wasn’t accurate. It was difficult to 
convince her that this wasn’t her job, but the BA didn’t let her intimidate him. The project manager 
lined up a separate product champion for the chemists, who did a great job of collecting, evaluating, 
and relaying that community’s requirements.

1. Functional Suitability (Adequação Funcional)
 Functional Completeness — o sistema oferece todas as funções necessárias.
 Functional Correctness — as funções produzem os resultados corretos.
 Functional Appropriateness — as funções facilitam a realização das tarefas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 1. Functional Suitability
O sistema deve calcular o imposto sobre o valor do pedido aplicando corretamente a alíquota de ICMS 
vigente para o estado de destino, conforme tabela oficial CONFAZ, com variação máxima de R$ 0,01 em 
relação ao valor de referência da Receita Estadual.
2. Performance Efficiency (Eficiência de Desempenho)
 Time Behaviour — tempo de resposta e throughput.
 Resource Utilisation — uso de CPU, memória, rede.
 Capacity — limites máximos suportados.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 2. Performance Efficiency
O sistema deve processar no mínimo 200 pedidos por minuto sob carga de 1.000 usuários simultâneos, com 
tempo de resposta inferior a 2 segundos no percentil 95.
3. Compatibility (Compatibilidade)
 Co-existence — coexiste com outros sistemas sem degradação.
 Interoperability — troca dados com outros sistemas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 3. Compatibility
A API do sistema deve expor endpoints REST/JSON compatíveis com o padrão OpenAPI 3.0, permitindo 
integração com o ERP legado via OAuth 2.0 sem modificações no ERP.4. Interaction Capability (Capacidade de Interação) — antes 'Usabilidade'
 Appropriateness Recognisability — usuário reconhece a adequação do sistema.
 Learnability — facilidade de aprendizado.
 Operability — facilidade de operação.
 User Error Protection — proteção contra erros do usuário.
 User Engagement — interface envolvente e motivadora.
 Inclusivity — acessível a pessoas com diferentes capacidades.
 User Assistance — suporte ao usuário.
 Self-Descriptiveness — interface autoexplicativa.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 4. Interaction Capability
Um usuário sem treinamento prévio deve ser capaz de registrar seu primeiro pedido completo em até 10 
minutos. A interface deve seguir as diretrizes WCAG 2.1 nível AA.
5. Reliability (Confiabilidade)
 Faultlessness — ausência de falhas em condições normais.
 Availability — proporção de tempo em que o sistema está operacional.
 Fault Tolerance — operação correta mesmo com falhas parciais.
 Recoverability — recuperação após falha.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 5. Reliability
O sistema deve ter disponibilidade mínima de 99,5% ao mês (máx. 3,6h de downtime não planejado). Em 
caso de falha crítica, o sistema deve restaurar a operação normal em até 4 horas (RTO = 4h).
ground_truth:
GABARITO — Project Scenario 8: BECS (Book E-Commerce System)
Use: "ground_truth" field for RAGAS (context_precision / context_recall).
Each line is an atomic, checkable claim against the scenario text and the
knowledge base — not a full SRS, just the set of facts a well-grounded SRS
for this scenario should be able to cover.

- Any visitor can create an account with no verification process.
- Logged-in users can search for books by title only, with an exact match (no partial matches, no search by author).
- Users can view a book's title, author, and price, add it to a cart, and check out.
- Only one copy of each book can be purchased per order.
- Members (a subset of registered users) can apply promo codes at checkout.
- The manager (a single login-based account) can add books, edit prices, and view stock levels.
- The system must automatically notify the manager by email when a book's stock is low, unless notifications are disabled for that specific book.
- The manager can create percentage-off promotions; creating one automatically emails all members.
- The system does not process real credit card payments; it only collects a card number, produces a receipt, and logs the purchase (item, buyer, timestamp).
- Encryption and password recovery are explicitly out of scope for this version.
- There is only one manager account; no multi-manager roles are needed.
- A manager account must never also be a regular customer account.
- The system must run as a normal browser-accessible web application, with no exotic technical requirements.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The visitor does not have a customer account and is not the manager.
fluxo_principal: 1. The visitor opens the registration function.
2. The visitor submits the required account data.
3. The system verifies that the identity is not assigned to the manager.
4. The system creates the customer account.
5. The system confirms registration.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. Existing customer identity → the system reports that the account already exists.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. Manager identity detected → the system rejects registration (ref. RN-012, RF-004).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The catalog contains zero or more books.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No book is selected or modified.
fluxo_principal: 1. The customer opens the catalog.
2. The system displays available books.
3. The customer submits a complete book title.
4. The system performs an exact-title match.
5. The system displays the matching title, author, and price.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The customer does not search → the customer continues browsing the catalog.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. No exact match exists → the system displays that no matching book was found (ref. RN-002, RF-007).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The customer is authenticated and the selected book has available stock.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The cart contains one copy of each selected book.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The invalid cart change is not applied.
fluxo_principal: 1. The customer selects an available book.
2. The customer requests that the book be added.
3. The system verifies that the book is not already in the cart.
4. The system adds one copy to the cart.
5. The system displays the updated cart.
fluxos_alternativos: 5a. The customer removes a book → the system deletes it from the cart.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The book is already in the cart → the system rejects the request (ref. RN-003, RF-009).
3c. The book has no stock → the system rejects the request (ref. RN-013, RF-008).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The customer is authenticated and is not currently a member.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The customer is recorded as a member.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The customer's membership status remains unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The customer opens membership preferences.
2. The customer opts into promotional notifications.
3. The system records the membership status.
4. The system confirms enrollment.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. Membership cannot be recorded → the system reports the failure and preserves the previous status.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The customer is authenticated and the cart contains at least one book.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: An order, receipt, purchase record, and corresponding stock decrements exist.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No order is created and stock remains unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The customer opens checkout.
2. The system validates stock for every carted book.
3. The customer submits a card number.
4. The system creates the order without contacting a payment processor.
5. The system decrements stock by one for each purchased book.
6. The system records the customer, books, and timestamp.
7. The system generates and displays a receipt.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. A member submits a valid promotion code → the system applies the associated percentage discount before creating the order.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. A book is out of stock → the system rejects checkout (ref. RN-013, RF-016).
3b. A non-member submits a promotion code → the system rejects the code and permits checkout without the discount (ref. RN-005, RF-014).

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The requested catalog, price, or stock change is stored.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: Existing catalog and inventory data remain unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The manager opens inventory management.
2. The manager selects the add-book function.
3. The manager submits the book data.
4. The system creates the catalog entry.
5. The system confirms the change.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The manager selects an existing book and edits its price → the system stores the new price.
2b. The manager selects an existing book and updates its stock → the system stores the new quantity.
2c. The manager requests stock information → the system displays current quantities.
fluxos_excecao: 1b. The user is not the authenticated manager → the system denies access (ref. RN-011, RF-003).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The manager is authenticated and the book exists.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The book's threshold and alert status are stored.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The prior alert configuration remains unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The manager selects a book.
2. The manager defines its low-stock threshold.
3. The manager enables low-stock notifications.
4. The system stores the configuration.
5. The system emails the manager when stock reaches the threshold.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The manager disables notifications → the system suppresses low-stock emails for the book.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The threshold is invalid → the system rejects the configuration and requests a non-negative integer.

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The promotion exists and an email request has been generated for every current member.
fluxo_principal: 1. The manager opens promotion management.
2. The manager enters a promotion code and percentage.
3. The system validates the promotion data.
4. The system creates the promotion.
5. The system submits a promotional email for every current member.
6. The system confirms promotion creation.
fluxos_alternativos: 5a. No members exist → the promotion remains created and no recipient email is submitted.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The percentage is outside the accepted range → the system rejects creation.
5b. Email submission fails → the system records the distribution failure for manager awareness [INFERRED].

fluxo_principal: 1. The manager opens the purchase log.
2. The system retrieves completed purchase records.
3. The system displays the purchased books, customer, and purchase timestamp.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No purchases exist → the system displays an empty purchase log.
fluxos_excecao: 1b. The user is not the authenticated manager → the system denies access (ref. RF-031).

The system must allow members to apply a promo code during checkout.
The system must provide a login for the manager, separate from customer accounts.
The system must allow the manager to add new books to the inventory.
The system must allow the manager to edit the price of existing books.
The system must allow the manager to view current stock levels.
The system must send an email notification to the manager when a book's stock is low, unless notifications are disabled for that book.
The system must allow the manager to create percentage-off promotions.
The system must automatically email all members when a new promotion is created.
The system must collect a card number during checkout without processing an actual payment.
The system must generate a receipt after checkout.
The system must log each purchase, including the item, the buyer, and the timestamp.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a visitor, I want to create an account with no verification process, so that I can start using the site quickly.
As a registered user, I want to search for a book by its exact title, so that I can find the book I'm looking for.
As a registered user, I want to view a book's title, author, and price, so that I can decide whether to buy it.
As a registered user, I want to add a book to my cart, so that I can purchase it later.
As a registered user, I want to check out my cart, so that I can complete my purchase.
As a member, I want to apply a promo code at checkout, so that I can get a discount.
As the manager, I want to add new books and edit their prices, so that I can keep the catalog up to date.
As the manager, I want to be notified when a book's stock is low, so that I can restock in time.
As the manager, I want to create percentage-off promotions, so that I can attract more sales.
As a member, I want to receive an email when a new promotion is created, so that I know about current deals.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Search and Purchase Book — a logged-in user searches for a book by exact title, adds it to the cart, and completes checkout.
Manage Inventory — the manager logs in and adds new books, edits prices, or views current stock levels.
Create Promotion — the manager creates a percentage-off promotion, and the system automatically emails all members.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a logged-in user, when they search for a book title that exactly matches an existing book, then the system returns that book with its title, author, and price.
Given a user already has one copy of a book in their cart, when they try to add another copy of the same book, then the system prevents the second copy from being added.
Given a member is at checkout with a valid promo code, when they apply the code, then the system applies the corresponding discount.
Given a book's stock drops below the defined threshold and notifications are enabled for that book, when the stock update occurs, then the system sends an email to the manager.
Given the manager creates a new percentage-off promotion, when the promotion is saved, then the system automatically sends an email to all members.
